notes:
These notes on Revelation 6 come from the pages I could reach. The rider on the white horse in verse 2 is where interpreters split most sharply. The split follows each teacher's overall approach to Revelation (future events, church history, or a picture of the whole church age) more than it follows denominations.

**Gaps:** I found nothing on Revelation 6 from the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Wesley's own commentary notes (only his translation of the verses), Pentecostal denominational sites (ag.org, pneumareview.com), Orthodox sources (oca.org), bibleodyssey.org, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those are left out. I also couldn't read the Bible Hub commentary pages for verses 15–17, so those verses mostly rely on Guzik.

---

**Overview: three main approaches**
- **Future events (futurist):** Guzik says that if you read Revelation as mostly *history*, you'll see this rider as Jesus, the apostles or the Roman emperors. If you read it as prophecy still to be fulfilled, you'll usually see him as the antichrist. He calls this rider "an interpretive crossroads" for the whole book. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/)
- **The whole church age (Reformed):** Ligonier says that as the seals are broken, we see the things that must take place throughout this era. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-black-and-pale-horses)
- **Church history (historicist):** Coffman reports Barnes's dating: 1st seal…..a period of great prosperity for the church until A.D. 180, with the later seals placed in the third century. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-6.html)

---

**v. 1**
- Only Jesus, the Lamb, had the right to break the seals. Each living creature is one of the cherubim of Ezekiel 1 and 10, and its "Come!" could also be translated "go forth," spoken to each horseman. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/)
- D. A. Carson compares the scroll to a first-century will: it is the slitting of the seals that enacts the document. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse-revelation-6/)
- **Text note (NET):** "and see," found in some older translations, was a later addition. "Come!" is better read as spoken to each horseman, and the shorter reading has the better manuscript support. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=6)

**v. 2 (the main point of disagreement)**
- **The antichrist (dispensational and Calvary Chapel teachers):** Guzik says Jesus does ride a white horse in Revelation 19, but *this* is a satanic dictator who imitates Jesus. He argues that the results of this rider's rule, in the verses that follow, show it is not Christ's reign. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/)
  - Chuck Smith places this right after the church is taken up: the antichrist comes forth on a white horse. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/6-2.html)
  - Gaebelein sees a counterfeit leader with a bow, but no arrow, whom he calls the "little horn" of Daniel 7. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/revelation-6.html)
  - Precept Austin links him to the false messiahs Jesus warned of in Matthew 24:4–5. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-6-commentary-supplement)
  - GotQuestions says he likely refers to the Antichrist. (https://www.gotquestions.org/four-horsemen-apocalypse.html)
- **Christ, or Christ going out in the gospel (older Protestant writers):**
  - Clarke: the white horse is the gospel and the rider is Jesus Christ.
  - Gill: Christ going out in the gospel, still conquering. He adds that it may also point to Vespasian, the Roman general God used against the Jews.
  - Coffman (Restoration Movement) follows the Reformed writer William Hendriksen in seeing "The Christ." He argues that a crown "given" by God cannot sit on an ungodly conqueror's head.
  - All three: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/6-2.html
- **Against the Christ reading:** Barnes says a horseman armed like this is not how Revelation usually pictures Christ. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/6-2.html)
- **War and military conquest (Reformed and evangelical scholars):**
  - Carson: Jesus is the Lamb here; he's not the horse. He says the white stands for military conquest. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse-revelation-6/)
  - Ligonier: conquering kings often rode white horses, and the horsemen picture God's judgment on His enemies, echoing Zechariah's horses. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/four-horsemen-apocalypse)
  - Barclay: the riders are forces of destruction, not particular historical figures. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/6-2.html)
- **NET notes (modern scholarship):** The NET lists three views: Christ, a spirit of military conquest, and the antichrist. It notes the two riders have little in common beyond the white horse; even the Greek word for "crown" differs. It judges the antichrist view the most probable one. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=6)

**vv. 3–4**
- Guzik says the rider only needed to *take away* peace, which is God's gift; war follows by itself. "Granted" shows this is God's judgment, directly or indirectly. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/)
- Carson says this is still under God's sanction, not God losing control. If the first horse suggests invasion from outside, the second may especially mean civil war. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse-revelation-6/)
- **Word note (NET):** the Greek verb for "slay" means to butcher or murder. "Fiery red" probably has a tinge of yellow or orange. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=6)

**v. 5**
- Carson says these are not the scales of justice. They are scales for weighing out money and food. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse-revelation-6/)
- Guzik says the scales show food being carefully rationed in a time of scarcity. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/)

**v. 6**
- **Prices:** Guzik says the prices are about twelve times normal, so a day's wage buys the makings of one loaf. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/) The NET says a quart was a daily ration for one person and a denarius was an average worker's daily pay. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=6) One commentary on Bible Hub notes that normally 16 to 20 measures sold for a denarius. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/6-6.htm)
- **"Do not harm the oil and wine":**
  - The common reading is that luxuries stay available while staples run short. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/; GotQuestions: https://www.gotquestions.org/four-horsemen-apocalypse.html)
  - Coffman disagrees: "Oil and wine were not luxuries, but part of the basic commodities of life." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/6-6.html)
  - Precept Austin notes the Greek command is singular, aimed at the rider, so God controls the judgment exactly. It also mentions other theories, such as weather that ruins grain but spares vines and olives. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-6-commentary)

**vv. 7–8**
- **The horse's colour (NET):** the Greek word means a sickly greenish-grey, the colour of someone ill. "With death" here can mean deadly disease. "Hades followed" means it was right behind. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=6)
- Carson calls it the color of a corpse. Because the sword and plagues overlap with the other horses, he argues the four are not separate periods of time. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse-revelation-6/)
- Guzik says the power is "given" by God, so God is in control even in the chaos. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/)
- Coffman says the four horsemen work throughout history until Christ returns: There is nothing in the text to suggest that they shall ever cease until the Second Advent. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-6.html)

**v. 9**
- **"Under the altar":** In the Old Testament, sacrificial blood was poured at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). The martyrs' lives are pictured as an offering to God. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/; Carson: https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse-revelation-6/)
- **Life after death:** Barnes calls this proof that the soul neither stops existing nor sleeps until the resurrection. The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary says the altar stands for Christ crucified. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/6-9.htm) Carson says calling them "souls" may point to the intermediate state, the time between death and resurrection. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse-revelation-6/)
- **Gill (historicist):** this seal is Diocletian's persecution, the last and greatest Roman one, and so includes all the martyrs before it. The altar may be Christ. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/6-9.htm)
- **Bible Hub verse page:** it shows the Christian mission can only go forward through suffering. Wordsworth cites Tertullian and Irenaeus: the souls rest until the resurrection rejoins them to their bodies. (https://biblehub.com/revelation/6-9.htm)
- Guzik says this is best taken as the cry of *all* martyrs, not only those of the end times. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/)
- **Catholic:** Haydock reports Jerome's view that the altar is Christ himself. He adds that the martyrs' souls live under Christ in heaven as their bodies are here deposited under our altars. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/hcc/revelation-6.html) Catholic Answers links this verse to the custom of sealing martyrs' relics inside church altars. (https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-altar)

**v. 10**
- **Asking for vengeance:** Guzik says the martyrs leave vengeance in God's hands and ask Him to do what He promised, like Abel's blood crying from the ground. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/) Carson admits many readers find this hard to square with Jesus' "Father, forgive them." He answers that God is assuring them His cause will be vindicated. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse-revelation-6/)
- Benson says the words mainly show how terrible the cruelty was, rather than a personal wish for revenge. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/6-9.htm)
- **Catholic:** Haydock and Challoner say the martyrs ask from zeal for God's glory, not hatred. They want God's justice seen so that persecutors may fear Him and turn to Him. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/hcc/revelation-6.html)
- **Word note (NET):** "Lord" here is *despotēs*, "Sovereign Master." (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=6)

**v. 11**
- **"The number of":** these words are supplied by translators. So the text may mean waiting until God's appointed martyrs are all killed, or until their character is complete. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/) The NET says a set "number" is implied by the Greek verb. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=6)
- Carson says the white robes stand for purity and blessedness. This is still not the final end. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-four-horsemen-of-the-apocalypse-revelation-6/)
- **Catholic:** Haydock uses the white robes to argue against the idea that the blessed do not see God before the final judgment. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/hcc/revelation-6.html)

**vv. 12–14**
- **The Old Testament background:** Guzik says cosmic signs like these go with the Messiah's coming in Isaiah, Joel, Zephaniah and Jesus' own teaching. He calls them best regarded as *real* but *poetic*. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/) The Cambridge Bible links them to Matthew 24:29, the signs just before Christ comes. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/6-12.htm)
- **Literal or symbolic:**
  - Coffman says these verses describe the Second Coming and the final judgment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/6-12.html)
  - Barnes calls it pure symbol, not to be looked for literally in history. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/6-12.htm)
  - Norris says this language is common in the Old Testament for revolutions and fallen governments. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/6-12.html)
- **Historicist readings:** Clarke suggests the "earthquake" is Constantine's conversion; Guzik says reading these events as history forces you to spiritualize them heavily. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/) One older commentary on Bible Hub reads the quake as a great change in the Roman Empire. Gill records that real earthquakes followed Diocletian's persecution. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/6-12.htm)
- **Word notes (NET):** the figs are late figs that often drop before ripening. The sky "was split" like a scroll being rolled up. "Like blood" means blood-red in colour. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=6)

**vv. 15–17**
- Guzik says every rank of person is equally brought low. He quotes Swete: what sinners fear most is not death but God's revealed presence. He quotes Torrance: the "wrath of the Lamb" is the wrath of sacrificial love. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-6/)
- Barnes (historicist) relates the panic of kings and great men to fear spreading through the Roman Empire at threats from the East and North. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/revelation/6-12.html)
